deep.reconstruction:
Context: Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792), end of Cap. 7 (orders of residues modulo d) and start of Cap. 8 (orders modulo a prime).

§240 (end). Let n be the least exponent with b^n ≡ 1 (mod d), i.e. ord_d(b) = n, and let bc = kd + 1, so bc ≡ 1. On the previous page Euler showed c^n ≡ 1, so the order of c is n or a proper divisor n/ν of n. Suppose c^{n/ν} ≡ 1. Then [my step] b^{n/ν} ≡ b^{n/ν}·(bc)^{n/ν} ... more simply (bc)^{n/ν} ≡ 1 gives b^{n/ν} ≡ 1, contradicting the minimality of n. Hence ord(c) = ord(b), i.e. ord(b^{-1}) = ord(b).

§241. Example with d = 13. Since 5^2 = 25 ≡ −1, we get 5^4 ≡ 1 with order 4. Solve 5c = 13k + 1. We need 13k + 1 ≡ 0 (mod 5), i.e. 3k ≡ 4, so k ≡ 3 (mod 5). Euler writes k = 5λ − 2, which gives c = 13λ − 5. The least value is c = 8, so 8 also has order 4 mod 13 (check: 8^2 = 64 ≡ −1).

§242. For each b < d coprime to d there is a c < d coprime to d with bc ≡ 1 (mod d). Existence is asserted here, presumably from earlier chapters. Uniqueness: if bc ≡ be ≡ 1, then d | b(c − e). Since gcd(b, d) = 1, d | c − e, and |c − e| < d forces c = e. The case c = b (self-inverse, b^2 ≡ 1) always occurs for b = 1 and b = d − 1.

Cap. VIII. Powers which leave remainder 1 on division by primes.

§243. (a + λd)^n ≡ a^n (mod d). For n even, (λd − a)^n ≡ a^n. So it suffices to study residues a < d.

§244. Let d = 2p + 1 be an odd prime, so φ(d) = 2p. For gcd(a, d) = 1, a^{2p} ≡ 1. This is Fermat's little theorem, proved earlier ("vidimus").

§245. If a^n ≡ 1 with n < 2p (the least such n is meant), then n | 2p. This is recalled from Ch. 7. Both a^{2p} − 1 and a^n − 1 are divisible by 2p + 1.

§246. If (2p+1) | a^n − 1, then (2p+1) | a^{mn} − 1. Hence (2p+1) | a^{mn} − a^{2p} = a^{2p}(a^{mn−2p} − 1). Since the prime does not divide a^{2p}, it divides a^{mn−2p} − 1, for any m (tacitly mn ≥ 2p).

§247. Let λ = gcd(n, 2p), n = αλ, 2p = βλ, with gcd(α, β) = 1. Both a^{αλ} − 1 and a^{βλ} − 1 are multiples of 2p + 1, hence so are a^{μαλ} − 1 and a^{νβλ} − 1. By Bézout, choose μ, ν with μα = νβ + 1. The difference (finished on the next page) is a^{νβλ+λ} − a^{νβλ} = a^{νβλ}(a^λ − 1). Therefore (2p+1) | a^λ − 1. In modern terms, a^n ≡ a^m ≡ 1 implies a^{gcd(n,m)} ≡ 1.
errors: No mathematical errors found; all numerical claims for d = 13 are correct (ord(5) = ord(8) = 4, and 5·8 = 40 = 3·13 + 1).
§242 asserts the existence of the inverse c without proof on this page; only uniqueness is proved here (existence presumably rests on earlier chapters).
§246 tacitly assumes mn ≥ 2p so that a^{mn−2p} is an integer power; harmless.
§240: the claim that the order of c is either n or a proper divisor of n relies on the previous page's c^n ≡ 1 together with the earlier result that the order divides any exponent giving 1.

results.what: ord_d(b^{-1}) = ord_d(b): if bc ≡ 1 (mod d), then b and c have the same multiplicative order
results.modern_name: An element and its inverse have the same order in (Z/dZ)^*

results.what: Existence and uniqueness of the modular inverse c < d of b coprime to d; self-inverse when b = 1 or d − 1
(a + λd)^n ≡ a^n, and (λd − a)^n ≡ a^n for n even
a^{p−1} ≡ 1 mod prime p, and the order divides p − 1
results.modern_name: Fermat's little theorem; Lagrange-type divisibility of the order
results.usually_credited_to: Fermat (1640, statement), Euler (1736 proof; 1758–1761 proof via residues/orders)

results.what: If a^n ≡ 1 and a^{2p} ≡ 1 (mod 2p + 1), then a^{gcd(n, 2p)} ≡ 1, via a Bézout relation μα = νβ + 1
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Theoremata circa divisores numerorum, c. 1750 / E134 and related)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (published 1849 in Opera Posthuma). The material — orders of residues, inverses, Fermat's little theorem, and the gcd argument — all appears in Euler's published memoirs and is standard.
